slides.title: What Are Landmarks? 🏛️
slides.content:
# Signposts for Screen Readers

HTML5 introduced several **landmark** elements that define major page areas. They automatically communicate their role to assistive technology.

Major landmarks:
- `<header>` – introductory content (site banner, not just a heading).
- `<nav>` – primary navigation.
- `<main>` – the unique content of the page (only one per page).
- `<footer>` – footer of the page or a section.
- `<aside>` – tangentially related content (sidebar, callout).
- `<section>` – thematic grouping of content (usually with a heading).

quizData.question: You can only have one `<header>` per HTML page.
quizData.explanation: Multiple `<header>` elements are allowed – they can be used for page header, article header, etc.

slides.title: `<main>` – The Heart of the Page ❤️
slides.content:
# Unique Content, Once Per Page The `
` element wraps the primary content that is unique to that document. It excludes repeated elements like site headers, navigation, footers. ```html

Latest Blog Posts

...
``` - Must not be nested inside other landmarks (except ``). - Screen readers can jump directly to `
` via a shortcut. A "skip to main content" link also targets it.

slides.title: `<nav>` – Primary Navigation Only ⚓
slides.content:
# Not Every Link List Use `
` for major navigation blocks, not for a list of links in a footer or sidebar unless those are primary. ```html
  • Home
  • About
``` Multiple `
` elements are fine; use `aria-label` to differentiate them.

slides.title: Landmarks in a Full Layout
slides.content: A typical page structure with all landmarks:
slides.codeSnippet:
My Blog

Home | Blog

Post Title

Content...

Related Posts

    ...

© 2025 My Blog

quizData.question: Which element is intended for the main unique content of a page?
quizData.explanation: `<main>` represents the dominant content of the document.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## `role="main"` is Implicit

`<main>` inherently has the ARIA role `main`, so you don't need to add it. However, if you must use a `<div>` as main (legacy browsers), add `role="main"`.
